who: James R. (James Randall) Jacob, historian of English science at CUNY; PhD in English history, Cornell.

evidence.says: LC identifies James Randall Jacob as James R. Jacob, professor of history at City University of New York, with a Cornell PhD in English history; it also records the form James Jacob.
The author biography identifies James R. Jacob as a retired history professor at John Jay College, CUNY, and author of Robert Boyle and the English Revolution and Henry Stubbe.

notes: The authority explicitly connects the shorter name, CUNY affiliation and Cornell doctorate. The precise doctorate year and Robin supervision were not independently verified.

who: Matthew F. Jacobs, University of Florida historian of US foreign relations; PhD UNC Chapel Hill, 2002.

evidence.says: Florida faculty biography gives a 2002 UNC Chapel Hill PhD in US history, specializing in foreign relations, and identifies his book Imagining the Middle East.
The departmental alumni directory lists Roger Carey, the dissertation Grinding It Out: Neoconservatives, Strategic Arms, and Protecting America, 1968-1980, and advisor Matthew Jacobs.
LC identifies Matthew F. Jacobs through his 2002 dissertation Constructing the Middle East, a PhD in the UNC Chapel Hill Department of History.

notes: Exact doctorate institution/year and direct departmental confirmation of the named student establish the match.

who: Wilbert L. Jenkins, Temple University historian of the Civil War and Reconstruction; PhD Michigan State.

evidence.says: LC identifies Wilbert L. Jenkins, also Wilbert Lee Jenkins, as the author of Seizing the New Day and an assistant professor of history at Temple.
Charles L. Nier III’s May 2011 Temple dissertation on credit discrimination and home ownership in Philadelphia lists Dr. Wilbert Jenkins, Professor of History, on its examining committee.
Temple’s History Department lists Wilbert L. Jenkins among its retired and emeritus faculty.
The reference entry identifies the Temple historian and author of Seizing the New Day, and reports a Michigan State PhD in 1989.

notes: The student’s dissertation and LC affiliation identify the same Temple historian. The reference entry gives 1989 for the PhD, whereas the supplied AHA record gives 1991; that year discrepancy remains unresolved.

who: Amelia M. Kiddle, University of Calgary historian of Mexico and Latin America; PhD Arizona, 2010.

evidence.says: Amelia M. Kiddle’s CV records a 2010 Arizona PhD in Latin American and World History, and Calgary history appointments beginning in 2012.
Hendrik Kraay’s CV lists David Barrios Giraldo’s 2021 Avatars of Memory dissertation with Dr. Amelia Kiddle as co-supervisor.
LC connects Amelia Kiddle, Amelia M. Kiddle and Amelia Marie Kiddle, identifying the Calgary history professor and author of Mexico’s Relations with Latin America during the Cárdenas Era.

notes: The full-name authority, exact doctorate and direct confirmation of the listed dissertation agree.

who: Thomas Miller Klubock, historian of modern Latin America at Stony Brook and subsequently Virginia; PhD history, Yale.

evidence.says: Thomas Miller Klubock’s CV gives a Yale history PhD, a Stony Brook associate professorship in 2001-2008, and Virginia appointments from 2008.
The approval page of Alberto Harambour-Ross’s May 2012 Stony Brook dissertation Borderland Sovereignties names Thomas Klubock, Professor at the University of Virginia, as dissertation co-advisor.
LC identifies Thomas Miller Klubock as author of Contested Communities and La Frontera.
Virginia identifies Thomas Klubock as Thomas Miller Klubock, a modern Latin American historian and author of La Frontera.

notes: Direct dissertation evidence explains the institutional timing: he co-advised the Stony Brook student after moving to Virginia. Yale institution verified; precise doctorate year not independently checked.

who: Stephen E. Koss, historian of modern Britain at Barnard and Columbia; PhD Columbia.
